<!-- slide template=title -->
# Chemical Equilibrium
The quantitative foundation: dynamic equilibrium, K, Q, and temperature

<!-- slide -->
## Learning objectives
1. Define chemical equilibrium as a dynamic state in which the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and the concentrations no longer change.
2. Write the equilibrium constant expression for a given balanced reaction, placing the products in the numerator and raising each concentration to its stoichiometric coefficient.
3. Evaluate the reaction quotient and compare it to the equilibrium constant to predict which direction the reaction will shift.
4. Explain why pure solids and pure liquids, whose activity is taken as one, are omitted from the equilibrium constant expression.
5. Relate the equilibrium constant to the standard Gibbs energy change using $\Delta G^\ominus = -RT \ln K$.
6. Predict how a change in temperature changes the equilibrium constant using the sign of the reaction enthalpy (the van 't Hoff relation).

<!-- slide template=outline -->
## What we will cover
- Equilibrium as a *dynamic* state, not a stopped one
- The equilibrium constant from a balanced equation
- The reaction quotient and the direction of change
- Why pure solids and liquids drop out
- The link to Gibbs energy
- Why only temperature changes $K$

<!-- slide template=section -->
## Dynamic equilibrium

<!-- slide -->
## Equal rates, not zero rates
At chemical equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions proceed at **equal, nonzero** rates,
so the reactant and product concentrations no longer change with time.

Nothing has stopped. The macroscopic composition is constant because two ceaseless processes
exactly balance.

<!-- slide -->
## Equilibrium is dynamic
Individual molecules keep reacting in both directions even though the measured concentrations
stay constant.

*Acetic acid in water:* a proton hops from an acetic acid molecule onto water and then onto an
acetate anion, remaking acetic acid. The count is unchanged; the reaction never stops.

<!-- slide template=section -->
## The equilibrium constant

<!-- slide -->
## Building K from a balanced equation
For $\ce{\alpha A + \beta B <=> \sigma S + \tau T}$:

$$K = \frac{[\ce{S}]^{\sigma}\,[\ce{T}]^{\tau}}{[\ce{A}]^{\alpha}\,[\ce{B}]^{\beta}}$$

Products in the numerator. Each concentration raised to its **stoichiometric coefficient**.

<!-- slide -->
## Where the form comes from
Guldberg and Waage's **law of mass action**: forward rate $k_{+}[\ce{A}]^{\alpha}[\ce{B}]^{\beta}$,
reverse rate $k_{-}[\ce{S}]^{\sigma}[\ce{T}]^{\tau}$.

Setting them equal at equilibrium gives $K = k_{+}/k_{-}$.

<!-- slide -->
## Pure solids and pure liquids
The terms in $K$ are strictly **activities**.

A pure solid or pure liquid has an **activity of one**, so it does not appear in the expression.
In dilute aqueous solution the solvent water is treated the same way.

<!-- slide template=section -->
## Predicting the direction of change

<!-- slide -->
## The reaction quotient
$Q_r$ has the same algebraic form as $K$, but is evaluated at **any** composition.

- $Q_r < K$ — too few products; shifts **forward**
- $Q_r > K$ — too many products; shifts **reverse**
- $Q_r = K$ — already at equilibrium; no net shift

<!-- slide template=section -->
## Equilibrium and thermodynamics

<!-- slide -->
## The link to Gibbs energy
Equilibrium is where the Gibbs energy of the system is at its minimum, so the reaction Gibbs
energy vanishes:

$$\Delta G^\ominus = -RT \ln K$$

Negative $\Delta G^\ominus$ corresponds to $K > 1$ (products favoured); positive to $K < 1$.

<!-- slide -->
## Only temperature changes K
$K$ is constant with respect to composition, but **depends on temperature** through the
**van 't Hoff equation**. The sign of the reaction enthalpy fixes the direction:

- **Endothermic** — raising $T$ **increases** $K$
- **Exothermic** — raising $T$ **decreases** $K$

<!-- slide -->
## Catalysts change neither
A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the **same factor**.

It shortens the time needed to *reach* equilibrium and changes **neither $K$ nor the position**
of equilibrium.

<!-- slide -->
## Watch out for these
- "At equilibrium the reactions have stopped" — the rates are equal but nonzero.
- "Concentrations are equal at equilibrium" — they are *constant*, generally unequal.
- "A catalyst raises the yield" — it changes neither $K$ nor the position.
- "Adding a pure solid changes $K$" — its activity is one, so it is absent.
- "Changing a concentration changes $K$" — only temperature changes $K$.

<!-- slide template=closing -->

which way does it move?
